opus-5.5.text:
I think by 2050 the dream is that we've moved biology from a largely empirical, trial-and-error discipline to something much closer to an engineering discipline, where you can actually predict what's going to happen before you go into the lab.

Right now, if you want to understand what a drug does to a cell, or what a particular mutation does to a tissue, you basically have to run the experiment, and often run it many times, in many contexts. It's slow and expensive, and most of what we try fails. What I'd love to see is a world where we have truly predictive models of biology, a virtual cell, and eventually virtual tissues and virtual organisms. You could ask a model, "If I perturb these three genes in this cell type, in this patient's genetic background, what happens?" and get an answer good enough that you only go to the wet lab to confirm it, not to search blindly.

Scientific superintelligence, to me, isn't a chatbot that summarizes papers really well. It's a system that can generate hypotheses humans wouldn't think of, design the experiments to test them, ideally run those experiments through automated labs, interpret the results, and close that loop over and over, much faster than a human-driven lab can. The models we're building today, DNA foundation models and generative models that can design proteins or even whole genomic elements, are early steps toward that. They're learning the language of biology directly from sequence and from large-scale perturbation data.

If we get it right, the payoff is enormous. We'd be curing diseases we currently treat as chronic or untreatable. We'd understand complex diseases like neurodegeneration, which involve many cell types interacting over decades, in a way we simply don't today. And we'd compress the timeline from a basic discovery to a therapy in a patient from fifteen or twenty years to something much shorter.

The part I think people underestimate is that it won't happen from models alone. You need the data-generation engine, the lab infrastructure, and the scientific culture to go with it. The bottleneck isn't just compute. It's whether we're measuring the right things at enough scale to teach these models how biology actually works. So by 2050, I'd hope we've built the AI and also rebuilt how we do experimental science around it.

r001.rationale: It describes generating hypotheses, designing and running experiments, interpreting results, and repeatedly closing the loop.

r002.rationale: It includes automated labs in that recurring loop and describes using wet-lab experiments to confirm model predictions.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the way I'd frame it is that I want scientific superintelligence to actually close the loop. Right now we have these incredible models that can read every paper, that can reason about biology, that can propose hypotheses, but there's still a human in the middle translating that into an experiment, running it on the bench, waiting three weeks, looking at the data, and then going back to the model. By 2050 I don't want that gap to exist. I want a system that can go from a question about how a disease works, to designing the experiment, to physically executing it in an automated lab, to interpreting the result, to updating its model of the world, and doing that thousands of times in parallel. That's what science actually is, it's that iterative loop, and the bottleneck has never really been ideas. It's been the cost and the speed of testing them.

The second thing is I don't want it to just be faster at what we already do. I want it to be able to operate in the parts of biology we fundamentally don't understand. If you look at where we are today, we can read genomes, we can edit genomes, but we still can't really write a cell from scratch and predict what it's going to do. The number of possible genetic programs is effectively infinite and we've explored a vanishingly small corner of it. A superintelligent scientist should be able to navigate that space, learn the rules of biology the way we eventually learned the rules of physics, and start engineering living systems with the same kind of design confidence we have for building a bridge or a chip.

And then the thing I care most about, honestly, is that it changes what medicine looks like. By 2050 I'd want most diseases that have a genetic basis to be addressable. Not managed, addressed. Where you can go from a patient's genome to a therapy that's designed for them, manufactured, and delivered on a timescale of weeks rather than decades. And that requires superintelligence not just in the reasoning layer, but embedded all the way down into the tools, the delivery vehicles, the manufacturing, the clinical trial design.

The last thing I'd say is that I think it has to be collaborative. I don't think the goal is to replace scientists. I think the goal is to make a grad student in 2050 have the leverage of an entire institute today. The best version of this is one where human curiosity is still setting the direction and the machine is just dramatically compressing the time it takes to find out whether you're right.

r001.rationale: Describes a repeated end-to-end loop from posing a question and designing an experiment through execution, interpreting results, and updating the model.

r002.rationale: Explicitly includes physically executing experiments in an automated lab as part of that loop.

astra-6.text:
By 2050, I’d love scientific superintelligence to help us move from describing biology to being able to predict and design it. We can collect enormous amounts of data about a cell, but we still struggle to predict what will happen when we change something. Imagine being able to move from an idea to a rigorous experiment to a useful treatment much more reliably.

I’d want these systems to participate in the whole scientific process: generate hypotheses, design experiments, learn from results, and recognize when their assumptions are wrong. The exciting part would be discovering things we didn’t even know to ask about, while grounding those discoveries in experiments we can check.

And I’d want that capability to be broadly accessible. A student with a great question should be able to pursue it without first assembling an enormous institution around themselves. For me, success would mean more people able to do ambitious science, and that science translating into healthier, longer lives.

r001.rationale: It describes a system participating in the whole scientific process—generating hypotheses, designing experiments, learning from results, and revising mistaken assumptions—communicating an iterative, end-to-end loop.

r002.rationale: It mentions designing and checking experiments, but does not communicate that a wet lab is integrated into the recursive loop.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d like scientific superintelligence to help us close the loop between asking a question, designing an experiment, and learning something real about the world. A system that can generate beautiful hypotheses is interesting, but I’d want it to test those hypotheses, recognize when they’re wrong, and revise its understanding.

By 2050, I’d hope we could give it an ambitious goal—like understanding how to repair a damaged tissue—and have it work with scientists across biology, chemistry, and engineering to make progress we can actually measure. The standard should be whether people live healthier lives and whether we understand nature more deeply.

And I’d want that capability to be broadly accessible. A student with a great question should be able to pursue it without needing the resources of a major institution. To me, that would be an exciting future: much more scientific capability, with many more people able to decide what questions are worth asking.

r001.rationale: The response describes a loop from asking questions to designing experiments, learning from results, and revising its understanding, which communicates an end-to-end recursive scientific method.

r002.rationale: It mentions designing and testing experiments with scientists, but does not communicate that a wet lab is integrated into the loop.
